moles-molar-mass-s1.title: Five samples on a balance
moles-molar-mass-s1.text: A student weighs five pure samples and looks up each molar mass.

table.caption: Mass and molar mass of each sample

moles-molar-mass-s2.title: Three boxes of gas particles
moles-molar-mass-s2.html: Key: small white circle, hydrogen atom; orange circle, oxygen atom; dark gray circle, carbon atom; light blue circle, neon atom. Molar masses: H₂O 18.02 g/mol, Ne 20.18 g/mol, CO₂ 44.01 g/mol.

items.q: What does one mole of a substance contain?
options: One gram of the substance, whatever it is made of
The number of atoms in one molecule of the substance
6.022 × 10²³ of the particles named, such as atoms or molecules
Enough of the substance to fill a 1-liter container

why.correct: One mole is Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, of whatever particles you name.
options: A mole is a count, not a mass. One mole of different substances has different masses.
That number is in the formula and is usually small, such as 3 for water.
Right: a mole is a counting unit, like a dozen, for 6.022 × 10²³ things.
A mole is a count of particles, not a volume.

items.q: How many moles of aluminum atoms are in Sample 1?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied the mass by the molar mass. Divide, so that grams cancel and moles are left.

why.correct: 13.5 g × (1 mol / 26.98 g) = 0.5004 mol, which is 0.500 mol to the three significant figures of the mass.

items.q: Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms in total?
options: Sample 3, the water
Sample 2, the copper
Sample 4, the ethanol
Sample 5, the sucrose

why.correct: Moles of atoms = moles of particles × atoms per particle. Sucrose: 0.250 × 45 = 11.3 mol; water 2.50 × 3 = 7.49 mol; copper 2.00 mol; ethanol 4.49 mol; aluminum 0.500 mol.
options: Water has the most molecules (2.50 mol), but only 3 atoms each, so 7.49 mol of atoms.
The largest mass, but copper atoms are heavy: 127 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol = 2.00 mol of atoms.
0.499 mol of molecules × 9 atoms each = 4.49 mol of atoms, less than sucrose or water.
Right: 85.6 g ÷ 342.30 g/mol = 0.250 mol of molecules, and each molecule has 45 atoms, so 11.3 mol of atoms.

items.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in Sample 4?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the number of ethanol molecules. Each molecule has 6 hydrogen atoms, so multiply by 6.

why.correct: 23.0 g ÷ 46.07 g/mol = 0.4992 mol of ethanol molecules. Each has 6 H atoms: 0.4992 × 6 = 2.995 mol of H atoms. × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.80 × 10²⁴ H atoms.

items.q: Sample 2 has about 9.4 times the mass of Sample 1 but only about 4.0 times as many atoms. Which statement explains this?
options: Copper atoms are packed closer together, so more fit in the sample
Each copper atom has about 2.4 times the mass of an aluminum atom
A mole of copper contains more atoms than a mole of aluminum
The copper mass has fewer significant figures, which lowers its count

why.correct: Mass = number of atoms × mass of each atom. Copper atoms are 63.55 / 26.98 = 2.36 times heavier, so 9.41 times the mass holds only 9.41 / 2.36 = 3.99 times the atoms.
options: How the atoms are packed changes the volume, not the mass per atom.
Every mole holds 6.022 × 10²³ particles, whatever the element.
Significant figures limit how precisely you report the count; they do not change it by a factor of two.

items.q: Which box holds the greatest mass of gas?
options: Box A, because its particles contain the most atoms
Box B, because it holds as many particles as Box A and each is heavier
The three boxes have equal masses
Box C, with 3 carbon dioxide molecules

why.correct: Total mass = number of particles × mass of each. A: 6 × 18.02 = 108.1 amu; B: 6 × 20.18 = 121.1 amu; C: 3 × 44.01 = 132.0 amu.
options: Box A has the most atoms (18), but they are light hydrogen and oxygen atoms: 108.1 amu in all.
Box B outweighs Box A, but Box C is heavier still.
The boxes hold different numbers of particles with different masses, so the totals differ.

items.q: Boxes A and B hold the same number of particles. How do their masses compare, and why?
options: Box B is heavier, because a neon atom has more mass than a water molecule
They have equal masses, because they hold equal numbers of particles
Box A is heavier, because each water molecule has three atoms
Box A is heavier, because water is a compound and neon is an element

why.correct: Same number of particles, so the box whose particles are heavier is heavier: 20.18 amu (Ne) > 18.02 amu (H₂O).
options: Right: 20.18 amu per neon atom against 18.02 amu per water molecule.
Equal numbers of particles have equal masses only if the particles have the same mass.
Counting atoms is not enough: one neon atom outweighs one O atom plus two light H atoms.
Being a compound says nothing about mass; the mass of each particle decides.

items.q: Which box contains the greatest number of atoms?
options: Box B
Box C
Box A
Boxes A and B, which tie

why.correct: Count atoms, not particles: A has 18, B has 6, C has 9.
options: Box B has 6 particles, but each is a single atom: 6 atoms.
3 molecules × 3 atoms = 9 atoms.
Right: 6 molecules × 3 atoms = 18 atoms.
They tie on particles (6 each), not on atoms (18 against 6).

items.q: Suppose each particle drawn stands for 0.100 mol of that substance. What mass of carbon dioxide does Box C represent?

mistakes.why: Value: that is one particle's worth. Box C has 3 particles, so 0.300 mol.
Value: you divided moles by molar mass. Multiply: mol × g/mol = g.
Value: you counted atoms (9) instead of molecules (3). Each CO₂ molecule is one particle of carbon dioxide.

why.correct: 3 particles × 0.100 mol = 0.300 mol of CO₂. 0.300 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 13.2 g.

items.q: What is the molar mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? Use Ca 40.08, C 12.01, O 16.00.

mistakes.why: Value: the subscript 3 applies to oxygen. Count three O atoms: 3 × 16.00 = 48.00.

why.correct: Add the atomic masses of every atom in one formula: 40.08 + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 100.09 g/mol.

items.q: What is the mass of 0.0250 mol of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (molar mass 180.16 g/mol)?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the molar mass. From moles to grams, multiply by g/mol.

why.correct: 0.0250 mol × (180.16 g / 1 mol) = 4.504 g, which is 4.50 g to three significant figures.

items.q: What is the mass, in grams, of a single water molecule (18.02 g/mol)?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by Avogadro's number. One molecule is a tiny fraction of a mole, so divide.

why.correct: 18.02 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 2.992 × 10⁻²³ g per molecule. A tiny number, as one molecule should be.

items.q: A flask holds 1.0 g of hydrogen gas, H₂, and another holds 1.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂. Which statement is correct?
options: Both flasks hold the same number of molecules, since the masses match
The hydrogen flask holds about 16 times as many molecules
The oxygen flask holds more molecules, since oxygen atoms are larger
The flasks need their volumes before they can be compared

why.correct: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass: H₂ 0.50 mol, O₂ 0.031 mol. The lighter the molecule, the more molecules in a gram.
options: Equal masses hold equal numbers only when the particles have the same mass.
Right: 1.0/2.016 = 0.50 mol of H₂ against 1.0/32.00 = 0.031 mol of O₂, a ratio of about 16.
Heavier molecules mean fewer of them in the same mass, not more.
Mass and molar mass are enough to find moles, and moles count molecules.

items.q: One molecule of ethanol has a mass of 46.07 amu. What is the mass of one mole of ethanol molecules?

why.correct: The number is the same at both scales: 46.07 amu per molecule and 46.07 g per mole. That is why the mole was defined as it was.
options: That is the mass of one molecule, not of 6.022 × 10²³ of them.
This multiplies twice: the g/mol number already counts a whole mole.
Dividing gives the mass of one molecule in grams, not of a mole.
Right: the mole is defined so that amu per particle equals grams per mole.

items.q: Which samples contain 1.00 mol of the particles named? Select all that apply.
options: 55.85 g of iron atoms (Fe, 55.85 g/mol)
1.00 g of hydrogen gas, counted as H₂ molecules
16.00 g of oxygen gas, counted as O₂ molecules
32.00 g of oxygen gas, counted as O₂ molecules
6.022 × 10²² water molecules

why.correct: One mole is the molar mass in grams, or 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Watch whether the particles are atoms or molecules.
options: Right: the molar mass in grams is one mole.
H₂ has a molar mass of 2.016 g/mol, so 1.00 g is 0.496 mol of molecules.
O₂ has a molar mass of 32.00 g/mol, so 16.00 g is 0.500 mol of molecules.
Right: 32.00 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 1.00 mol of O₂ molecules.
That is one tenth of Avogadro's number, 0.100 mol.

items.q: Four flasks each hold 1.0 g of a gas. Put them in order from the fewest moles to the most.
options: CO₂ (44.01 g/mol)
O₂ (32.00 g/mol)
CH₄ (16.04 g/mol)
H₂ (2.016 g/mol)

why.correct: With the same mass, moles = 1.0 g ÷ molar mass, so the heaviest molecule gives the fewest moles: CO₂ 0.023, O₂ 0.031, CH₄ 0.062, H₂ 0.50 mol.

items.q: A 50.0 g sample of water (18.02 g/mol) is replaced by 50.0 g of methane, CH₄ (16.04 g/mol). Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Number of molecules
variables.why: Methane molecules are lighter, so 50.0 g holds more of them: 3.12 mol against 2.77 mol.

variables.name: Mass of the sample
variables.why: Both samples are 50.0 g by design.

variables.name: Total number of atoms
variables.why: More molecules, and 5 atoms each instead of 3: 15.6 mol of atoms against 8.32 mol.

why.correct: Same mass, lighter molecules: more molecules. Each methane molecule also has more atoms, so the atom count rises even more.

items.q: A student reports that 2.0 g of helium (4.003 g/mol) contains 4.8 × 10²⁴ atoms. Which quick check shows the answer is wrong?
options: 2.0 g is about half a mole, so it should be about 3 × 10²³ atoms
Helium is a gas, so it has fewer atoms than a solid of the same mass
A count of atoms is at most 6.022 × 10²³, one mole
The answer should have units of grams, not atoms

why.correct: 2.0 g × (1 mol / 4.003 g) × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ atoms. The student multiplied by the molar mass (2.0 × 4.003 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 4.8 × 10²⁴).
options: Right: 2.0 ÷ 4.0 ≈ 0.5 mol, and half of 6 × 10²³ is 3 × 10²³. The reported answer is 16 times too big.
Being a gas changes how spread out the atoms are, not how many are in 2.0 g.
Samples larger than a mole hold more than 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
A count of atoms has no mass unit; the question asks for a number of atoms.
